item.title: Measurements of the neutron background for the Colorado Underground Research Institute (CURIE)
item.description: arXiv:2610.31856v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the first direct measurements of the neutron background at the Colorado Underground Research Institute (CURIE), a shallow-underground facility with an effective overburden of approximately $400$~m.w.e.\ in the Edgar Experimental Mine in Idaho Springs, Colorado. The radiogenic and muon-induced components were characterized in the Subatomic Particle Hideout. The radiogenic component was measured with a custom Bonner Cylinder Spectrometer comprising a $^{3}$He proportional counter and six cylindrical high-density polyethylene moderators. Its response functions were simulated in \textsc{geant4}, empirically calibrated using a $^{239}$Pu-$^{9}$Be source and the shadow-cone method, and then corrected to account for the approximately isotropic underground field. Unfolding the measured count rates gives a total local scalar neutron flux, dominated by radiogenic production, for $E_n\lesssim\SI{10}{\MeV}$ of $(2.51\pm0.58_{\rm stat}\pm0.39_{\rm sys})\times10^{-5}$~\si{\per\square\centi\meter\per\second}. The muon-induced component was measured with a BC-501A organic liquid scintillator operated for \SI{1431}{\hour}. Pulse shape discrimination identified 55~$\pm$~7 neutron candidates. Using the simulated detector response, these counts yield an integral muon-induced neutron flux at the rock--cavern boundary above \SI{10.5}{\MeV} of $(2.09\pm0.29_{\rm stat}\,{}^{+0.79}_{-0.53}{}_{\rm sys})\times10^{-7}$~\si{\per\square\centi\meter\per\second}. This flux uses the first-entry, boundary-area normalization of a previous CURIE simulation study. Its central value is approximately \SI{12}{\percent} higher than the site-specific prediction but is consistent within the reported uncertainties. Together, these measurements characterize the radiogenic and high-energy cosmogenic neutron environments at CURIE and provide quantitative input for planning future low-background experiments at the facility.
item.dc:creator: Dakota K. Keblbeck, Uwe Greife, Eric Mayotte, Wouter Van De Pontseele, Kyle G. Leach

item.title: Development of an Analog Front-End Using NINO ASIC for Mini-ICAL
item.description: arXiv:2610.32619v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The mini-ICAL was supposed to be a pre-prototype detector of the Iron CALorimeter (ICAL) of the India-based Neutrino Observatory (INO) project. Resistive Plate Chamber (RPC) was the active element of these detectors. As this detector operates in avalanche mode, one needs a very fast pre-amplifier for signal processing. NINO ASIC developed for the ALICE time-of-flight detector was a potential chip to be used as the analog-front end. This paper presents an 8-in-1 pre-amplifier board developed using the NINO ASIC, a single-ended to differential signal conversion using the differential driver chip manufactured by Texas Instruments, production of the boards, lessons learned during production, testing of these boards, and interface with RPCs. Finally, its performance based on strip rates and efficiency of the detector will also be discussed.
item.dc:creator: Ravindra R Shinde, Punnet Kanwar Kaur, Gobinda Majumder, S Pethuraj, K C Ravindran, Mandar Saraf, B Satyanarayana

item.title: A Large-Volume GAGG(Ce) Detector Module for In-Beam $\gamma$-Ray Spectroscopy
item.description: arXiv:2610.32621v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We report on the development and characterization of large-volume GAGG(Ce) scintillation detector modules equipped with silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) readout. Each module houses four large-volume GAGG(Ce) crystals within a compact thin carbon-fiber enclosure, minimizing the passive material budget and enabling the construction of high-efficiency, large-solid-angle detector arrays for in-beam $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy. The performance of 10 GAGG modules (40 detectors), including the energy linearity, energy and timing resolution, and intrinsic full-energy peak efficiency, was evaluated using standard $\gamma$-ray sources and $^{14}$N(p,$\gamma$)$^{15}$O reactions, covering a $\gamma$-ray energy range from about 0.3 MeV to 8 MeV. Non-linear energy response across the measured energy range was observed due to the non-linear response of the SiPM. The detector modules exhibit good energy resolution (FWHM below 5\% at 1.33 MeV), good timing resolution (FWHM $\sim$500 ps at $\sim$1 MeV), and intrinsic full-energy peak efficiencies in good agreement with Geant4 simulations, making the detector modules a promising solution for next-generation high efficiency in-beam $\gamma$-ray experiments at RI-beam facilities.

item.title: Radiation damage and recovery of SiPMs exposed to low-momentum muon beams for innovative scintillation-based muon beam monitors
item.description: arXiv:2610.32852v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Silicon PhotoMultipliers (SiPMs) are among the standard devices for light detection in scintillator detectors. Some detector designs require these devices to be placed in radioactive areas or directly exposed to particle beams. Specifically, the damage from exposure to low-momentum muons is particularly important, as they have a high energy deposit and they have several applications in material science and particle physics. Eight SiPM models from different manufacturers were exposed to 29 MeV/c positive muons, with an intensity of O(10^6) muons/s for 13 hours, maximising the charge deposited in the depletion region. I-V curves were measured before/after irradiation and annealing; DCR and crosstalk analyses are ongoing, to extract dark count rate and optical crosstalk. Despite showing a measurable increase in dark current, the devices preserved operational stability. Thermal annealing has also been tested by heating the devices at 125{\deg}C, showing a recovery of the optimal SiPM features. This work is part of a collaboration between the University of Pavia and ISIS, to develop detectors for low-momentum muons (< 40 MeV/c), based on thin scintillators.

item.title: The scintillating fibre beam monitor for the CHNet-MAXI experiment at ISIS: characterisation of the light collection and detection system
item.description: arXiv:2610.32865v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The CHNet-MAXI experiment at ISIS aims at a non-destructive isotopic characterisation of lead samples, based on muonic atom formation. A custom scintillation-based detector is used for the reconstruction of the time and space distributions of the low-energy muon beam employed in the experiment. The beam monitor consists of two orthogonal planes of 10 cm-long, 3 mm $\times$ 3 mm square scintillating fibres, totalling 64 fibres, read out by four arrays of 16 Hamamatsu S14160-3015PS SiPMs each. The optical performance of the detector has been characterised, focusing on the SiPM behaviour, and also checking and correcting the uniformity of the light response across channels with a $^{60}$ Co source. A first detector test with protons at the CNAO-XPR has been carried out. The results of the Geant4 simulation of the detector, fundamental for the detector operation and data analysis, are also presented. All these activities are preliminary to the final detector operation in the CHNet-MAXI experiment at the RIKEN-RAL Port4 decay muon beamline at ISIS.

item.title: Electron Wavefronts Capture Nanoscale Movies of Hypersound at Surfaces
item.description: arXiv:2610.32419v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Acoustic waves transport mechanical energy and elastic strain through solids, with material composition and shape governing their propagation. In the gigahertz hypersound regime, acoustic wavelengths reach tens to hundreds of nanometres, comparable to nanoscale device dimensions. Harnessing these waves underpins high-frequency signal processing, sensing, electromagnetic coupling and quantum control. Acoustic metrology probes elastic modes and internal interfaces. Yet directly imaging how nanoscale acoustic waves interact with local structure remains challenging, requiring picometre displacement sensitivity combined with high spatiotemporal resolution. Here we demonstrate full-field imaging of laser-induced hypersound at surfaces using reflected electron wavefronts. We introduce ultrafast low-energy electron microscopy (ULEEM), exploiting the intrinsic surface sensitivity of few-electronvolt electrons. Coherent electron pulses down to femtosecond durations reflect from the topmost atomic layers, imprinting the evolving surface profile onto their wavefronts. Defocus converts phase variations into image contrast. In a thin van der Waals material, we image the thermoelastic generation and propagation of picometre-amplitude acoustic waves. Measured dispersion relations, interpreted through elastodynamic modelling, distinguish substrate-supported and locally detached regions, revealing how interfacial contact shapes propagation. Delayed wave emission reveals scattering at buried mechanical defects. Our results establish electron-wavefront imaging of nanoscale surface dynamics, enabling the exploration of ultrafast energy transport, structural transformations and coupled mechanical, electronic and magnetic phenomena.
item.dc:creator: Johannes Otto, Leon Brauns, Benjamin Schroeder, Claus Ropers

item.title: From Hollow Waveguides to Mie Voids: Low-Index Light Confinement
item.description: arXiv:2610.32494v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The confinement of light within optically thin media challenges the conventional view that optical localization requires high-index dielectric materials and total internal reflection. Over the past decades, a broad range of photonic phenomena has demonstrated that electromagnetic energy can also be guided and localized inside low-index regions or nanoscale void cavities. What first appears to be a curiosity is, in fact, highly relevant: The interaction between light and matter lies at the heart of much in optics and photonics. It enables sensing, nonlinear optical phenomena, and optical manipulation, yet it also inevitably introduces absorption, dissipation, and loss. Pushing localized, enhanced, or guided energy into a lower-index space thus offers entirely new possibilities for light-matter interaction and dispersion control. In this review, we discuss some of these counterintuitive structures, starting with light guidance within optically thin media, such as hollow-core photonic crystal fibers or antiresonant reflecting optical waveguides. We then discuss the optics of bubbles, that is, low-index inclusions in a higher-index surrounding, and ultimately arrive at the so-called Mie void resonators, optical resonators that support localized electromagnetic modes confined within a region of lower refractive index. All these systems demonstrate that there are (resonant) optics beyond simple total internal reflection. Absence can itself become a functional photonic degree of freedom, opening opportunities across sensing, quantum nanophotonics, metasurfaces, and programmable optical matter.
item.dc:creator: Dominik Ludescher, Ivan Toftul, Harald Giessen, Yuri Kivshar, Mario Hentschel

item.title: Analytical model for the photomultiplier single photoelectron response including the electron back-scattering contribution
item.description: arXiv:2604.02826v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Many models exist to describe the single photoelectron response of photomultipliers. Generally to describe the spectral region between the fully amplified primary photoelectron peak and the electronics pedestal an ad hoc function is used (often an exponentially modified gaussian) without a clear physical justification. In this paper, following the physical description of back-scattered primary photoelectrons at the first dynode described in the "The Photomultiplier Handbook" by A.~G. Wright published by Oxford University Press, we derive an analytical function describing these partially amplified primary photoelectrons. This function depends only on intrinsic parameters of the photomultiplier such as the gain at the first dynode and the intrinsic resolution of the dynode chain following the first. Furthermore, analytical descriptions of the fully amplified peak and very low charge signals are derived. The model has been successfully validated with data from two different photomultipliers acquired with a low-noise amplifier.

item.title: Gamma Neutron Radioactive Source Identification in Water Cherenkov Detectors
item.description: arXiv:2608.06518v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Water Cherenkov Detectors (WCDs) are a robust technology widely used in astrophysics, high energy physics, and recently nuclear security applications. They detect high energy interactions through the Cherenkov light emitted by charged particles traveling faster than the speed of light in water. In this work, we demonstrate the feasibility of gamma-neutron discrimination in WCDs using a combined methodology that integrates statistical analysis with machine learning techniques. The experimental setup employs different shielding configurations to isolate gamma and neutron contributions from a \textsuperscript{241}AmBe source, while \textsuperscript{60}Co and \textsuperscript{137}Cs sources are used to establish a signal to energy calibration. A statistical analysis based on a $3\sigma$ significance criterion is used to define energy thresholds, enabling a linear relationship between the measured charge spectrum and the deposited energy. Building on this calibration, pulse shape information is further exploited through machine learning methods to improve event classification. An ensemble model based on a soft-voting strategy combining a Bagging classifier, CatBoost, and a Multilayer Perceptron was trained on detector signals acquired under different shielding conditions, achieving an accuracy of 0.816 and an area under the Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve. The combined approach demonstrates that statistical thresholding provides a physically grounded discrimination baseline across the full energy range, while machine learning enhances classification performance at higher energies by leveraging pulse level information. This integrated strategy improves radiation identification capabilities in water Cherenkov detectors, with potential applications in nuclear security and radiation detection.
item.dc:creator: A. N\'u\~nez Selin, C. Sarmiento Cano, H. Asorey, I. Sidelnik

item.title: QubiC 2.0: An Extensible Open-Source Qubit Control System Capable of Mid-Circuit Measurement and Feed-Forward
item.description: arXiv:2309.10333v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Researchers manipulate and measure quantum processing units via the classical electronics control system. We developed an open-source FPGA-based quantum bit control system called QubiC for superconducting qubits. After years of qubit calibration and testing experience on QubiC 1.0, we recognized the need for mid-circuit measurement and feed-forward capabilities to implement advanced quantum algorithms, and upgraded the system to QubiC 2.0 on an AMD ZCU216 RFSoC evaluation board with all these enriched features. The system uses portable FPGA gateware with a simplified processor to handle commands on-the-fly. For design simplicity and straightforward scaling, we adopted a multi-core distributed architecture, assigning one processor core per qubit. The pulses combine the unique pulse envelope and carrier information specified in a command. Each pulse envelope is pre-stored in the FPGA's block RAMs, ensuring speed and reusability throughout the quantum circuit, while pulse parameters including amplitude, phase, and frequency can be updated from pulse to pulse. The software stack is developed in Python, running on both the FPGA's ARM core and a host computer via XML-RPC. Quantum circuits can be described in a high-level language supporting both pulse-level and native-gate-level programming with high-level control flow constructs, and are compiled into binary commands loaded into the FPGA. With QubiC 2.0, we achieved multi-FPGA synchronization and low-latency data communication, and demonstrated feed-forward experiments on conditional circuits. The system also serves as a platform for artificial intelligence and machine learning driven quantum control, such as FPGA-based real-time quantum state discrimination. The enhanced QubiC system provides researchers with powerful tools to explore and implement advanced quantum algorithms and applications.

item.title: Universal Boolean Computation in Negatively Coupled Circle Map Lattices
item.description: arXiv:2610.16290v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We investigate the computational capabilities of a one-dimensional lattice of negatively coupled circle maps in its traveling wave regime. We interpret propagating waves as information carriers and exploit their interactions to implement Boolean logic. The logical states are encoded by the propagation direction of the traveling waves, while the presence or absence of a wave at a designated output location represents the logical output. Using controlled wave collisions, we demonstrate the realization of NAND and NOR gates along with other basic gates. Since NAND and NOR operations are functionally complete, the results establish that the traveling wave regime of the negatively coupled circle-map lattice supports universal Boolean computation in principle. The demonstrated logical operations remain valid over a finite range of the coupling strength \epsilon and map parameter \omega, indicating robustness of the computational scheme to parameter variations. Our results therefore demonstrate that computational functionality can emerge from the collective nonlinear dynamics of a coupled map lattice, providing a con- nection between the dynamical properties of traveling wave states and collision based information processing.
item.dc:creator: Priyanka D. Bhoyar, Prashant M. Gade
